## Finding unobserved groups

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/index/03-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/index.qmd; note-sha256: eafdf3f74dd9f55976b1f4316ebdfea38cc94171723aa772ca34d1b1a06e8527; role: concept -->

One row is one recorded vowel token; rows repeat speakers, elicitation words, and intended vowels.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Peterson and Barney's vowel-production study recorded repeated /hVd/ productions and their acoustic measurements. This unit uses the table distributed as `phonTools::pb52` in package version 0.2.2.2. The package is BSD-licensed, though those package terms do not separately establish redistribution terms for the historical table. One row is one recorded vowel token; rows repeat speakers, elicitation words, and intended vowels.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html
https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html
:::

## Finding unobserved groups

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/index/04-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/index.qmd; note-sha256: eafdf3f74dd9f55976b1f4316ebdfea38cc94171723aa772ca34d1b1a06e8527; role: concept -->

The linguistic question is whether recurring regions appear in this acoustic representation and, if so, how they relate to categories supplied by the experimental design.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The fitting representation contains F1 and F2 but not the elicitation word or intended-vowel label. The linguistic question is whether recurring regions appear in this acoustic representation and, if so, how they relate to categories supplied by the experimental design.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html
https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html
:::

## Finding unobserved groups

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/index/05-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/index.qmd; note-sha256: eafdf3f74dd9f55976b1f4316ebdfea38cc94171723aa772ca34d1b1a06e8527; role: concept -->

That interpretation requires a separate comparison with linguistic metadata or held-out measurements.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A group is unobserved only in the sense that no group label is supplied to the fitting procedure. A fitted cluster or mixture component is not automatically a phoneme, a vowel category, or a speaker type. That interpretation requires a separate comparison with linguistic metadata or held-out measurements.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html
https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html
:::

## Hard clustering

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/index/06-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/index.qmd; note-sha256: eafdf3f74dd9f55976b1f4316ebdfea38cc94171723aa772ca34d1b1a06e8527; role: concept -->

Because F1 and F2 have different empirical spreads, the transformation affects the geometry supplied to the clustering algorithm.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The analysis begins by representing each object as a row of measurements. Distance and scaling then determine which token pairs count as similar. Because F1 and F2 have different empirical spreads, the transformation affects the geometry supplied to the clustering algorithm.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html
https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html
:::

## Hard clustering

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/index/07-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/index.qmd; note-sha256: eafdf3f74dd9f55976b1f4316ebdfea38cc94171723aa772ca34d1b1a06e8527; role: concept -->

Validation without outcome labels then asks how centroids estimated from other speakers reconstruct a complete unseen-speaker panel.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

K-means assigns each token to one cluster and represents each cluster by a centroid. The assignment and centroid updates minimize within-cluster loss. Silhouette widths compare each token's distance to its assigned cluster with its distance to the nearest alternative. Validation without outcome labels then asks how centroids estimated from other speakers reconstruct a complete unseen-speaker panel.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html
https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html
:::

## Finite mixture models

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/index/08-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/index.qmd; note-sha256: eafdf3f74dd9f55976b1f4316ebdfea38cc94171723aa772ca34d1b1a06e8527; role: concept -->

Posterior membership probabilities quantify how much each component contributes to the density at an observed token, and expectation--maximization alternates between updating these responsibilities and the component parameters.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **finite mixture model** represents a distribution as a weighted combination of component distributions. A Gaussian mixture uses Gaussian components for the acoustic measurements. Posterior membership probabilities quantify how much each component contributes to the density at an observed token, and expectation--maximization alternates between updating these responsibilities and the component parameters.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html
https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html
:::

## Finite mixture models

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/index/09-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/index.qmd; note-sha256: eafdf3f74dd9f55976b1f4316ebdfea38cc94171723aa772ca34d1b1a06e8527; role: concept -->

Held-out mixture validation then evaluates fitted density for speakers absent during fitting and uses intended vowels only for a separate post-fit alignment check.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Choosing a mixture with BIC compares fitted likelihoods after accounting for parameter count. BIC still treats token rows as likelihood contributions, so the repeated-speaker structure remains a limitation rather than disappearing into the criterion. Held-out mixture validation then evaluates fitted density for speakers absent during fitting and uses intended vowels only for a separate post-fit alignment check.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html
https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html
:::

## Validation and sequence

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/index/10-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/index.qmd; note-sha256: eafdf3f74dd9f55976b1f4316ebdfea38cc94171723aa772ca34d1b1a06e8527; role: concept -->

The probability calculations rely on random variables and distributions, while both validation analyses reuse the separation between training and test data.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This distinction between statistical components and linguistic categories fixes the interpretation throughout the sequence. The pages thus specify (i) the represented object and geometry, (ii) the hard-clustering objective and its held-out target, and (iii) the probabilistic mixture objective and its held-out target. The probability calculations rely on random variables and distributions, while both validation analyses reuse the separation between training and test data.

Peterson and Barney recorded repeated productions of ten /hVd/ words from adult and child speakers, then measured the fundamental frequency and the first three formants in a steady-state vowel section. The package table contains no listener-level response, session, or seat variables from the paper’s perception experiment.

[Transcript]

The audited table has 1,520 token rows from 76 speakers. Each speaker contributes 20 rows: two repetitions of each of ten elicitation words. ## Defining the represented objects {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/representing-objects/05-math; notes-page: latent-structure/representing-objects.qmd; note-sha256: f990228bda1e82014e40c5ece9723fc12ac7def6332d0c54bcdebe8d348d9fef; role: math -->

Let $N$ linguistic objects be measured on $p$ numerical properties. Their representation is

$$
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_1^{\mathsf T}\\
\vdots\\
\mathbf{x}_N^{\mathsf T}
\end{bmatrix}
\in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_1^{\mathsf T}\\
\vdots\\
\mathbf{x}_N^{\mathsf T}
\end{bmatrix}
\in
\mathbb{R}^{N\times p}.
$$

## Repeated rows change the target

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/representing-objects/11-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/representing-objects.qmd; note-sha256: f990228bda1e82014e40c5ece9723fc12ac7def6332d0c54bcdebe8d348d9fef; role: concept -->

Averaging all 20 rows for each speaker would produce a grouping of speakers and remove the within-speaker vowel space almost entirely.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Treating the 1,520 tokens as rows produces a grouping of productions. Averaging each speaker-vowel pair first would instead produce 760 speaker-vowel means and remove repetition-level variation. Averaging all 20 rows for each speaker would produce a grouping of speakers and remove the within-speaker vowel space almost entirely.

## What the representation omits

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/representing-objects/13-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/representing-objects.qmd; note-sha256: f990228bda1e82014e40c5ece9723fc12ac7def6332d0c54bcdebe8d348d9fef; role: concept -->

Restricting the matrix to F1 and F2 is thus a teaching choice, not a claim that the other measurements are irrelevant.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Peterson and Barney also measured F0 and F3. F3 is especially relevant to the rhotic vowel, while a steady-state section cannot capture every dynamic property of an /hVd/ word. Restricting the matrix to F1 and F2 is thus a teaching choice, not a claim that the other measurements are irrelevant.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html
https://www.fon.hum.uva.nl/praat/manual/Create_formant_table__Peterson___Barney_1952_.html
:::

## What the representation omits

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/representing-objects/14-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/representing-objects.qmd; note-sha256: f990228bda1e82014e40c5ece9723fc12ac7def6332d0c54bcdebe8d348d9fef; role: concept -->

Our clustering is a descriptive reanalysis of the released production table.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The paper used the measurements to examine experimental control, production variation, and the relation between acoustic patterns and listener classifications. It did not fit K-means or Gaussian mixtures. Our clustering is a descriptive reanalysis of the released production table.

## Distance and scaling

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling/02-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling.qmd; note-sha256: c5a2ed553d7b6c03de12c4410336b49cff59d040370580de85c51b90f83bbf85; role: concept -->

Here we compare raw hertz, global standardization, and a speaker-relative representation before fixing the geometry used on later pages.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The Peterson-Barney table introduced on the preceding page gives F1 and F2 in hertz. A distance calculation must state how those two measurements become one comparison. Here we compare raw hertz, global standardization, and a speaker-relative representation before fixing the geometry used on later pages.

## Euclidean distance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling/03-math; notes-page: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling.qmd; note-sha256: c5a2ed553d7b6c03de12c4410336b49cff59d040370580de85c51b90f83bbf85; role: math -->

For two rows $\mathbf{x}_i$ and $\mathbf{x}_{i'}$ with $p$ features, **Euclidean distance** is

$$
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_{i'})
=
\sqrt{
\sum_{m=1}^{p}
(x_{im}-x_{i'm})^2
}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For two rows $\mathbf{x}_i$ and $\mathbf{x}_{i'}$ with $p$ features, **Euclidean distance** is

$$
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_{i'})
=
\sqrt{
\sum_{m=1}^{p}
(x_{im}-x_{i'm})^2
}.
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Euclidean distance

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling/04-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling.qmd; note-sha256: c5a2ed553d7b6c03de12c4410336b49cff59d040370580de85c51b90f83bbf85; role: concept -->

The units of that geometry come from the feature transformation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Subtracting within columns keeps the comparison feature-specific. Squaring makes positive and negative differences contribute in the same direction, and adding gives an axis-aligned geometry. The units of that geometry come from the feature transformation.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Euclidean distance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling/05-math; notes-page: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling.qmd; note-sha256: c5a2ed553d7b6c03de12c4410336b49cff59d040370580de85c51b90f83bbf85; role: math -->

For the main representation, we standardize within speaker:

$$
z_{isj}
=
\frac{F_{isj}-\bar F_{sj}}{s_{sj}},
\qquad j\in\{1,2\},
$$

where $\bar F_{sj}$ and $s_{sj}$ are the mean and sample standard deviation across speaker $s$’s 20 tokens.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For the main representation, we standardize within speaker:

$$
z_{isj}
=
\frac{F_{isj}-\bar F_{sj}}{s_{sj}},
\qquad j\in\{1,2\},
$$

where $\bar F_{sj}$ and $s_{sj}$ are the mean and sample standard deviation across speaker $s$’s 20 tokens.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

Distance becomes

$$
d(i,i')
=
\sqrt{
(z_{i1}-z_{i'1})^2+(z_{i2}-z_{i'2})^2
}.
$$

## Comparing the induced neighborhoods

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling/10-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling.qmd; note-sha256: c5a2ed553d7b6c03de12c4410336b49cff59d040370580de85c51b90f83bbf85; role: concept -->

This post hoc comparison suggests that the speaker-relative geometry reduces a salient speaker-type organization while increasing alignment with the elicitation labels.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Under raw hertz, 70.5% of nearest neighbors share intended-vowel metadata and 63.3% share speaker type. In the within-speaker geometry, those rates are 89.7% and 41.2%, respectively. This post hoc comparison suggests that the speaker-relative geometry reduces a salient speaker-type organization while increasing alignment with the elicitation labels.

## The prediction information set

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling/12-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling.qmd; note-sha256: c5a2ed553d7b6c03de12c4410336b49cff59d040370580de85c51b90f83bbf85; role: concept -->

No held-out token estimates a centroid or mixture component, but held-out measurements do determine their speaker's coordinate system.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Within-speaker standardization uses a speaker's complete unlabeled 20-token panel to determine that speaker's mean and standard deviation. The later speaker-blocked analyses thus target a new speaker whose complete calibration panel is available. No held-out token estimates a centroid or mixture component, but held-out measurements do determine their speaker's coordinate system.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14

It also leaves dependence among the 20 transformed rows unmodeled.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This distinction follows the prediction information set. The analysis does not predict one isolated token from a speaker with no calibration data. It also leaves dependence among the 20 transformed rows unmodeled.

## Scaling does not establish relevance

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling/14-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling.qmd; note-sha256: c5a2ed553d7b6c03de12c4410336b49cff59d040370580de85c51b90f83bbf85; role: concept -->

A duplicated feature would receive double influence, while an omitted dynamic or F3 measurement receives none.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Standardization gives each chosen coordinate a comparable observed spread. It does not make F1 and F2 equally reliable, independent, or exhaustive. A duplicated feature would receive double influence, while an omitted dynamic or F3 measurement receives none.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Scaling does not establish relevance

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling/15-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/distance-and-scaling.qmd; note-sha256: c5a2ed553d7b6c03de12c4410336b49cff59d040370580de85c51b90f83bbf85; role: concept -->

A high-quality clustering under this geometry may summarize recurring F1-F2 regions, but it cannot establish that this geometry captures every linguistically relevant relation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus, Euclidean distance remains conditional on the representation. A high-quality clustering under this geometry may summarize recurring F1-F2 regions, but it cannot establish that this geometry captures every linguistically relevant relation.

## K-means clustering {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/02-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: concept -->

We fix $K=10$ only to compare a ten-centroid acoustic partition with the experiment's ten elicitation categories after fitting; this is not a claim that K-means discovered the category count.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We now fit centroids to the speaker-relative Peterson-Barney representation. Intended-vowel labels do not enter the fit. We fix $K=10$ only to compare a ten-centroid acoustic partition with the experiment's ten elicitation categories after fitting; this is not a claim that K-means discovered the category count.

## Assignments, centroids, and loss {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/03-math; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: math -->

Let $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^p$ be token $i$'s feature vector. For $K$ clusters, let

$$
z_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}
$$

be its hard assignment and let

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\in\mathbb{R}^p
$$

be centroid $k$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^p$ be token $i$'s feature vector. For $K$ clusters, let

$$
z_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}
$$

be its hard assignment and let

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\in\mathbb{R}^p
$$

be centroid $k$.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Assignments, centroids, and loss {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/04-math; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: math -->

**K-means clustering** minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares

$$
W
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z_i}
\right\rVert^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

**K-means clustering** minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares

$$
W
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z_i}
\right\rVert^2.
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Assignments, centroids, and loss {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/05-math; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: math -->

For fixed centroids, the assignment step chooses

$$
z_i
=
\underset{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k
\right\rVert^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For fixed centroids, the assignment step chooses

$$
z_i
=
\underset{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k
\right\rVert^2.
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Assignments, centroids, and loss {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/06-math; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: math -->

For fixed assignments, the update step replaces each centroid with the mean of its assigned rows:

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k
=
\frac{1}{|C_k|}
\sum_{i\in C_k}\mathbf{x}_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For fixed assignments, the update step replaces each centroid with the mean of its assigned rows:

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k
=
\frac{1}{|C_k|}
\sum_{i\in C_k}\mathbf{x}_i.
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Why the update is a mean {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/07-math; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: math -->

For one coordinate of one fixed cluster, the squared loss around a proposed center $\mu$ is

$$
Q(\mu)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For one coordinate of one fixed cluster, the squared loss around a proposed center $\mu$ is

$$
Q(\mu)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^2.
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Why the update is a mean {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/08-math; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: math -->

Its derivative is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}\mu}
=
-2\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Its derivative is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}\mu}
=
-2\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu).
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Why the update is a mean {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/09-math; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: math -->

Setting this derivative to zero gives

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i-n\mu=0,
$$

and thus

$$
\mu
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Setting this derivative to zero gives

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i-n\mu=0,
$$

and thus

$$
\mu
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i.
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Why the update is a mean

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/10-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: concept -->

The coordinatewise mean thus minimizes squared distance for fixed assignments.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The coordinatewise mean thus minimizes squared distance for fixed assignments.

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14

It does not turn a centroid into a vowel, establish perceptual validity, or make the analysis supervised.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The adjusted Rand index (ARI) against the withheld intended-vowel metadata is 0.755. This number measures alignment between two partitions after the acoustic fit. It does not turn a centroid into a vowel, establish perceptual validity, or make the analysis supervised.

## Alternation and local solutions

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/17-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: concept -->

The procedure thus decreases or preserves the objective until it reaches a local solution.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Each assignment step cannot increase $W$ because every token chooses its nearest current centroid. Each update step cannot increase $W$ because each centroid becomes the mean of its assigned rows. The procedure thus decreases or preserves the objective until it reaches a local solution.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Alternation and local solutions

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/k-means/18-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/k-means.qmd; note-sha256: ee94d306c90ad2817bac883b31092da276d60936d69d0c06e94b8d6ec5d71f87; role: concept -->

A poor fit would diagnose this representation and objective, not the absence of organization in the production data.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

K-means favors compact regions under squared Euclidean distance and assigns every token to exactly one region. Overlapping productions may not have that structure. A poor fit would diagnose this representation and objective, not the absence of organization in the production data.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Within-cluster loss

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss/02-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.qmd; note-sha256: 1724603de2e95e1fe3dc4a3b35218339185b811a6f0ea086a2f950edc39bdce6; role: concept -->

We now trace the training loss across a declared grid using the same speaker-relative Peterson-Barney representation, seed policy, and multi-start fitting rule at every count.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

K-means requires a centroid count before fitting. We now trace the training loss across a declared grid using the same speaker-relative Peterson-Barney representation, seed policy, and multi-start fitting rule at every count.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Loss at a declared centroid count {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss/03-math; notes-page: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.qmd; note-sha256: 1724603de2e95e1fe3dc4a3b35218339185b811a6f0ea086a2f950edc39bdce6; role: math -->

For the K-means fit with $K$ centroids, write

$$
W_K
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z_i,K}
\right\rVert^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For the K-means fit with $K$ centroids, write

$$
W_K
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left\lVert
\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z_i,K}
\right\rVert^2.
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Loss at a declared centroid count {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss/04-math; notes-page: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.qmd; note-sha256: 1724603de2e95e1fe3dc4a3b35218339185b811a6f0ea086a2f950edc39bdce6; role: math -->

The subscript records that both assignments and centroids were estimated under candidate count $K$. The reduction obtained by adding centroid $K$ is

$$
\Delta_K
=
W_{K-1}-W_K,
\qquad K\geq2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The subscript records that both assignments and centroids were estimated under candidate count $K$. The reduction obtained by adding centroid $K$ is

$$
\Delta_K
=
W_{K-1}-W_K,
\qquad K\geq2.
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Loss at a declared centroid count

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss/05-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.qmd; note-sha256: 1724603de2e95e1fe3dc4a3b35218339185b811a6f0ea086a2f950edc39bdce6; role: concept -->

A larger $\Delta_K$ means that the additional centroid removes more squared reconstruction error from the fitted rows.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A larger $\Delta_K$ means that the additional centroid removes more squared reconstruction error from the fitted rows.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Why the optimal curve cannot rise {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss/06-math; notes-page: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.qmd; note-sha256: 1724603de2e95e1fe3dc4a3b35218339185b811a6f0ea086a2f950edc39bdce6; role: math -->

A model with $K+1$ centroids can reproduce a $K$-centroid solution by duplicating one existing center and retaining the assignments. Since the larger model can do at least this well,

$$
W_{K+1}\leq W_K.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A model with $K+1$ centroids can reproduce a $K$-centroid solution by duplicating one existing center and retaining the assignments. Since the larger model can do at least this well,

$$
W_{K+1}\leq W_K.
$$

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Why the optimal curve cannot rise

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss/07-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.qmd; note-sha256: 1724603de2e95e1fe3dc4a3b35218339185b811a6f0ea086a2f950edc39bdce6; role: concept -->

A computed curve can rise after a poor local solution; multiple starts reduce this algorithmic failure without changing the mathematical relation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus, the globally minimized training loss reaches its smallest value at the largest permitted $K$. A computed curve can rise after a poor local solution; multiple starts reduce this algorithmic failure without changing the mathematical relation.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## The elbow is a visual judgment

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss/10-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.qmd; note-sha256: 1724603de2e95e1fe3dc4a3b35218339185b811a6f0ea086a2f950edc39bdce6; role: concept -->

The Peterson-Barney curve supplies real reductions, but it does not supply a universal cutoff for what counts as small.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An **elbow plot** displays $W_K$ against $K$. The **elbow method** looks for a count after which additional centroids produce much smaller reductions. The Peterson-Barney curve supplies real reductions, but it does not supply a universal cutoff for what counts as small.

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14

## Loss remains tied to the representation

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss/12-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.qmd; note-sha256: 1724603de2e95e1fe3dc4a3b35218339185b811a6f0ea086a2f950edc39bdce6; role: concept -->

Duplicating F2 would give it twice the influence.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Within-cluster loss depends on feature units, columns, and row count. Replacing speaker-relative scores with raw hertz would change the vertical scale and could change the fitted partitions. Duplicating F2 would give it twice the influence.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Loss remains tied to the representation

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss/13-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/within-cluster-loss.qmd; note-sha256: 1724603de2e95e1fe3dc4a3b35218339185b811a6f0ea086a2f950edc39bdce6; role: concept -->

The monotone loss curve cannot decide that one count is linguistically correct merely by reaching a minimum.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Training compactness also does not establish a vowel inventory. Every additional centroid increases representational capacity on the same observations used to estimate it. The monotone loss curve cannot decide that one count is linguistically correct merely by reaching a minimum.

[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14
:::

## Silhouette widths

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/silhouette-scores/02-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/silhouette-scores.qmd; note-sha256: 378f45be4c7ef9a1904bc74f30e22e4d5e41abf06b573bb4777b6d572513daf1; role: concept -->

A **silhouette width**90125-7) compares within-cluster cohesion with the nearest alternative.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The within-cluster loss measures distance from each token to its assigned centroid. It does not ask whether the token is nearly as close to another fitted group. A **silhouette width**90125-7) compares within-cluster cohesion with the nearest alternative.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1016/0377-0427(87
:::

## Cohesion and the nearest alternative {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/silhouette-scores/03-math; notes-page: latent-structure/silhouette-scores.qmd; note-sha256: 378f45be4c7ef9a1904bc74f30e22e4d5e41abf06b573bb4777b6d572513daf1; role: math -->

Let $C(i)$ be the cluster containing token $i$. Its average distance to the other rows in that cluster is

$$
a(i)
=
\frac{1}{|C(i)|-1}
\sum_{j\in C(i),\ j\neq i}
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $C(i)$ be the cluster containing token $i$. Its average distance to the other rows in that cluster is

$$
a(i)
=
\frac{1}{|C(i)|-1}
\sum_{j\in C(i),\ j\neq i}
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j).
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1016/0377-0427(87
:::

## Cohesion and the nearest alternative {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/silhouette-scores/04-math; notes-page: latent-structure/silhouette-scores.qmd; note-sha256: 378f45be4c7ef9a1904bc74f30e22e4d5e41abf06b573bb4777b6d572513daf1; role: math -->

For another cluster $C$, define

$$
d(i,C)
=
\frac{1}{|C|}
\sum_{j\in C}
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For another cluster $C$, define

$$
d(i,C)
=
\frac{1}{|C|}
\sum_{j\in C}
d(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j).
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1016/0377-0427(87
:::

## Cohesion and the nearest alternative {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/silhouette-scores/05-math; notes-page: latent-structure/silhouette-scores.qmd; note-sha256: 378f45be4c7ef9a1904bc74f30e22e4d5e41abf06b573bb4777b6d572513daf1; role: math -->

The nearest alternative-cluster distance is

$$
b(i)
=
\min_{C\neq C(i)}d(i,C).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The nearest alternative-cluster distance is

$$
b(i)
=
\min_{C\neq C(i)}d(i,C).
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1016/0377-0427(87
:::

## Cohesion and the nearest alternative {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/silhouette-scores/06-math; notes-page: latent-structure/silhouette-scores.qmd; note-sha256: 378f45be4c7ef9a1904bc74f30e22e4d5e41abf06b573bb4777b6d572513daf1; role: math -->

The silhouette width is

$$
s(i)
=
\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The silhouette width is

$$
s(i)
=
\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}.
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1016/0377-0427(87
:::

## Cohesion and the nearest alternative {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/silhouette-scores/07-math; notes-page: latent-structure/silhouette-scores.qmd; note-sha256: 378f45be4c7ef9a1904bc74f30e22e4d5e41abf06b573bb4777b6d572513daf1; role: math -->

If $b(i)\geq a(i)$, then

$$
s(i)=1-\frac{a(i)}{b(i)},
$$

which lies between zero and one.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $b(i)\geq a(i)$, then

$$
s(i)=1-\frac{a(i)}{b(i)},
$$

which lies between zero and one.

:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/silhouette-scores/08-math; notes-page: latent-structure/silhouette-scores.qmd; note-sha256: 378f45be4c7ef9a1904bc74f30e22e4d5e41abf06b573bb4777b6d572513daf1; role: math -->

If $a(i)>b(i)$, then

$$
s(i)=\frac{b(i)}{a(i)}-1,
$$

which lies between minus one and zero.

## Reconstructing one observed silhouette

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/silhouette-scores/10-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/silhouette-scores.qmd; note-sha256: 378f45be4c7ef9a1904bc74f30e22e4d5e41abf06b573bb4777b6d572513daf1; role: concept -->

## Limits of the score

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/silhouette-scores/16-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/silhouette-scores.qmd; note-sha256: 378f45be4c7ef9a1904bc74f30e22e4d5e41abf06b573bb4777b6d572513daf1; role: concept -->

A singleton cluster conventionally receives silhouette zero because within-cluster cohesion cannot be estimated from a pair.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Silhouettes inherit the distance, scaling, and fitted partition. Compact groups separated by gaps tend to score well, while systematically overlapping categories may not. A singleton cluster conventionally receives silhouette zero because within-cluster cohesion cannot be estimated from a pair.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1016/0377-0427(87
:::

## Why reconstruction loss does not select a category count

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/unsupervised-validation/12-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/unsupervised-validation.qmd; note-sha256: 584b5792786b85c775a00a055c5b35c1833be288b70c20b0e59e73d425cfdf3a; role: concept -->

Finite training samples and local optimization may make a validation curve wiggle, but the target still rewards added representational capacity.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A codebook with $K+1$ centers can reproduce a $K$-center codebook by duplicating one center. Its population reconstruction loss can thus decrease or remain constant as capacity increases. Finite training samples and local optimization may make a validation curve wiggle, but the target still rewards added representational capacity.

[Sources]

Course note: latent-structure/unsupervised-validation.qmd
:::

It does not estimate a phonological inventory by itself.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Held-out loss can compare how efficiently declared codebook sizes represent new panels, or it can be paired with a separately declared complexity budget. It does not estimate a phonological inventory by itself.

## Gaussian mixtures

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures/02-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.qmd; note-sha256: d3e1e19ae743a3c8dff61c8a4d89f35e12a07c61c0a5946c23978a3847eab982; role: concept -->

A **Gaussian mixture model (GMM)** instead represents regions by weighted probability distributions, each with an estimated location and spread.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The Peterson-Barney production space contains overlapping F1-F2 regions. K-means represents each region by one point and assigns every token to exactly one centroid. A **Gaussian mixture model (GMM)** instead represents regions by weighted probability distributions, each with an estimated location and spread.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## One Gaussian component {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures/03-math; notes-page: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.qmd; note-sha256: d3e1e19ae743a3c8dff61c8a4d89f35e12a07c61c0a5946c23978a3847eab982; role: math -->

Let $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^p$ be token $i$'s measurements. Component $k$ has mean

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\in\mathbb{R}^p
$$

and covariance

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^p$ be token $i$'s measurements. Component $k$ has mean

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\in\mathbb{R}^p
$$

and covariance

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}.
$$

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## One Gaussian component {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures/04-math; notes-page: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.qmd; note-sha256: d3e1e19ae743a3c8dff61c8a4d89f35e12a07c61c0a5946c23978a3847eab982; role: math -->

Its density is

$$
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)
=
\frac{
\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{2}
(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^{\mathsf T}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}
(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k)
\right]
}{
(2\pi)^{p/2}|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k|^{1/2}
}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Its density is

$$
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)
=
\frac{
\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{2}
(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^{\mathsf T}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}
(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k)
\right]
}{
(2\pi)^{p/2}|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k|^{1/2}
}.
$$

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## One Gaussian component {.equation-slide}

## Fitting the declared ten-component model

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures/10-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.qmd; note-sha256: d3e1e19ae743a3c8dff61c8a4d89f35e12a07c61c0a5946c23978a3847eab982; role: concept -->

Thus, covariance ellipses are axis-aligned, share a determinant, and may allocate their spread differently between the two formant dimensions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We fix a ten-component `EVI` covariance family before fitting. In `mclust`, `EVI` is diagonal with equal volume and varying shape. Thus, covariance ellipses are axis-aligned, share a determinant, and may allocate their spread differently between the two formant dimensions.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

These are model checks, not linguistic interpretations of the component numbers.

## Post-fit alignment and uncertainty

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures/14-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.qmd; note-sha256: d3e1e19ae743a3c8dff61c8a4d89f35e12a07c61c0a5946c23978a3847eab982; role: concept -->

The latter summarizes how much posterior mass remains outside the most probable component.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The hard component assignments have ARI 0.801 against the withheld intended-vowel metadata, while mean classification uncertainty is 0.071. The former describes post-fit alignment. The latter summarizes how much posterior mass remains outside the most probable component.

## Components are not phonemes

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures/15-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.qmd; note-sha256: d3e1e19ae743a3c8dff61c8a4d89f35e12a07c61c0a5946c23978a3847eab982; role: concept -->

Several components may cover productions from one elicitation category, and one component may cover overlapping productions from several categories.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A fitted Gaussian component is a distributional object under the chosen measurements, transformation, component count, and covariance restriction. Several components may cover productions from one elicitation category, and one component may cover overlapping productions from several categories.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## Components are not phonemes

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures/16-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.qmd; note-sha256: d3e1e19ae743a3c8dff61c8a4d89f35e12a07c61c0a5946c23978a3847eab982; role: concept -->

Post-fit alignment cannot eliminate that limitation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The speaker-relative transformation may reduce anatomy-related differences, but it can also remove sociolinguistically relevant variation. Moreover, F3 and dynamic information remain outside the model. A potential worry is thus that a sharp component reflects an incomplete acoustic representation. Post-fit alignment cannot eliminate that limitation.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## Covariance collapse

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures/17-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.qmd; note-sha256: d3e1e19ae743a3c8dff61c8a4d89f35e12a07c61c0a5946c23978a3847eab982; role: concept -->

Positive-definiteness checks, covariance restrictions, and fitting diagnostics must precede interpretation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An unrestricted Gaussian component can concentrate around very few rows while its covariance approaches singularity. The likelihood may then grow without representing a recurring acoustic region. Positive-definiteness checks, covariance restrictions, and fitting diagnostics must precede interpretation.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## Covariance collapse

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures/18-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/gaussian-mixtures.qmd; note-sha256: d3e1e19ae743a3c8dff61c8a4d89f35e12a07c61c0a5946c23978a3847eab982; role: concept -->

It does not establish that every acoustic region truly has diagonal covariance.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The `EVI` restriction used here limits the fitted geometry. It does not establish that every acoustic region truly has diagonal covariance.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html

The **posterior probability of component membership**, often expressed as **responsibilities**, applies Bayes' rule inside the fitted mixture.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A Gaussian mixture assigns density to every observed acoustic vector. We now ask how the weighted component contributions divide for one Peterson-Barney token. The **posterior probability of component membership**, often expressed as **responsibilities**, applies Bayes' rule inside the fitted mixture.

Before observing $\mathbf{x}_i$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(Z_i=k)=\pi_k.
$$

## Conditioning on an unobserved component {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/posterior-membership/06-math; notes-page: latent-structure/posterior-membership.qmd; note-sha256: b2b2140449ab0d906ab4c58da790911cfa89c6bcef7926555da92f911de1361a; role: math -->

Conditional on component $k$,

$$
f(\mathbf{x}_i\mid Z_i=k)
=
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k).
$$

::: {.notes}

Conditional on component $k$,

$$
f(\mathbf{x}_i\mid Z_i=k)
=
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k).
$$

## Conditioning on an unobserved component {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/posterior-membership/07-math; notes-page: latent-structure/posterior-membership.qmd; note-sha256: b2b2140449ab0d906ab4c58da790911cfa89c6bcef7926555da92f911de1361a; role: math -->

Bayes' rule gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(Z_i=k\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\frac{
\mathbb{P}(Z_i=k)f(\mathbf{x}_i\mid Z_i=k)
}{
f(\mathbf{x}_i)
}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Bayes' rule gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(Z_i=k\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\frac{
\mathbb{P}(Z_i=k)f(\mathbf{x}_i\mid Z_i=k)
}{
f(\mathbf{x}_i)
}.
$$

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14

r_{ik}
=

}{
\sum_{j=1}^{K}
\pi_j\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_j,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)
}.
$$

::: {.notes}

Substituting the mixture density yields

r_{ik}

## Expectation-maximization

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/expectation-maximization/02-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/expectation-maximization.qmd; note-sha256: e378781beb2731946fe6e625c0a5928e2b47716dd4fd4961eaa550d329b874eb; role: concept -->

The **expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm** alternates those two calculations when neither side is known.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If component labels were observed, we could estimate a Gaussian from its assigned Peterson-Barney tokens. If component parameters were known, we could calculate each token's responsibilities. The **expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm** alternates those two calculations when neither side is known.

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}

\right\}_{k=1}^{K}.
$$

If component label $Z_i$ were observed, define

$$
I_{ik}=\mathbf{1}[Z_i=k].
$$

## Complete and observed data {.equation-slide}

\ell_{\mathrm{complete}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})

\right].
$$

## The expectation step {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/expectation-maximization/07-math; notes-page: latent-structure/expectation-maximization.qmd; note-sha256: e378781beb2731946fe6e625c0a5928e2b47716dd4fd4961eaa550d329b874eb; role: math -->

Given $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}$, calculate

$$
r_{ik}^{(t)}
=
\mathbb{P}(Z_i=k\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
=
\frac{
\pi_k^{(t)}
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{(t)})
}{
\sum_{j=1}^{K}
\pi_j^{(t)}
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_j^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j^{(t)})
}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Given $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}$, calculate

$$
r_{ik}^{(t)}
=
\mathbb{P}(Z_i=k\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
=
\frac{
\pi_k^{(t)}
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{(t)})
}{
\sum_{j=1}^{K}
\pi_j^{(t)}
\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_j^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j^{(t)})
}.
$$

[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html
:::

## The expectation step {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/expectation-maximization/08-math; notes-page: latent-structure/expectation-maximization.qmd; note-sha256: e378781beb2731946fe6e625c0a5928e2b47716dd4fd4961eaa550d329b874eb; role: math -->

Since

$$
\mathbb{E}[I_{ik}\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}]
=r_{ik}^{(t)},
$$

the EM auxiliary objective is

$$
Q(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)})
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}
r_{ik}^{(t)}
\left[
\log\pi_k+
\log\mathcal{N}
(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)
\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Since

$$
\mathbb{E}[I_{ik}\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}]
=r_{ik}^{(t)},
$$

the EM auxiliary objective is

=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}
r_{ik}^{(t)}

\log\pi_k+

(\mathbf{x}_i;\boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)

## The maximization step {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/expectation-maximization/10-math; notes-page: latent-structure/expectation-maximization.qmd; note-sha256: e378781beb2731946fe6e625c0a5928e2b47716dd4fd4961eaa550d329b874eb; role: math -->

The effective token count for component $k$ is

$$
N_k^{(t)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{ik}^{(t)}.
$$

::: {.notes}

The effective token count for component $k$ is

=

## The maximization step {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/expectation-maximization/11-math; notes-page: latent-structure/expectation-maximization.qmd; note-sha256: e378781beb2731946fe6e625c0a5928e2b47716dd4fd4961eaa550d329b874eb; role: math -->

The updated weight and mean are

$$
\pi_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{N_k^{(t)}}{N}
$$

and

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{1}{N_k^{(t)}}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{ik}^{(t)}\mathbf{x}_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The updated weight and mean are

$$
\pi_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{N_k^{(t)}}{N}
$$

and

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{1}{N_k^{(t)}}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{ik}^{(t)}\mathbf{x}_i.
$$

## The maximization step {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/expectation-maximization/12-math; notes-page: latent-structure/expectation-maximization.qmd; note-sha256: e378781beb2731946fe6e625c0a5928e2b47716dd4fd4961eaa550d329b874eb; role: math -->

For an unrestricted Gaussian component, the covariance update is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{1}{N_k^{(t)}}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
r_{ik}^{(t)}
\left(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t+1)}\right)
\left(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t+1)}\right)^{\mathsf T}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For an unrestricted Gaussian component, the covariance update is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{1}{N_k^{(t)}}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
r_{ik}^{(t)}
\left(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t+1)}\right)
\left(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{(t+1)}\right)^{\mathsf T}.
$$

## Local solutions and variance constraints

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/expectation-maximization/19-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/expectation-maximization.qmd; note-sha256: e378781beb2731946fe6e625c0a5928e2b47716dd4fd4961eaa550d329b874eb; role: concept -->

Without such protection, a component may collapse around very few tokens and yield a misleadingly large likelihood.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The variance floor prevents an estimated diagonal variance from approaching zero. It is a declared computational constraint, not an observed linguistic variance. Without such protection, a component may collapse around very few tokens and yield a misleadingly large likelihood.

A fixed seed reproduces the collection of starts; it does not make the first solution globally best.

::: {.notes}

## Choosing a mixture with BIC

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture/02-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 643dad72ef0160bdfe257ca9c4073edd5f2d4d170c7512abaaf020126e46066b; role: concept -->

A Gaussian mixture requires both a component count and a covariance family.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A Gaussian mixture requires both a component count and a covariance family. We use the **Bayesian information criterion (BIC)** to compare a declared grid on the speaker-relative Peterson-Barney representation, then distinguish the selected distributional model from the ten-component model used to teach membership and external alignment.

The covariance families and component range are fixed before intended-vowel agreement is inspected. A candidate specification contains the component count $K$, covariance family $\mathcal C$, and remaining procedure $\mathcal R$:

M=\langle K,\mathcal C,\mathcal R\rangle.
$$

## BIC and its sign convention {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture/05-math; notes-page: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 643dad72ef0160bdfe257ca9c4073edd5f2d4d170c7512abaaf020126e46066b; role: math -->

For maximized likelihood $L$, $q$ estimated parameters, and $n$ likelihood contributions, define

$$
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\log L+q\log n.
$$

For maximized likelihood $L$, $q$ estimated parameters, and $n$ likelihood contributions, define

$$

=

## BIC and its sign convention {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture/06-math; notes-page: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 643dad72ef0160bdfe257ca9c4073edd5f2d4d170c7512abaaf020126e46066b; role: math -->

Smaller values are preferred under this convention. `mclust` reports the negative quantity,

$$
\operatorname{BIC}_{\texttt{mclust}}
=
2\log L-q\log n,
$$

so its larger value is better.

## Interpreting the sample size

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture/12-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 643dad72ef0160bdfe257ca9c4073edd5f2d4d170c7512abaaf020126e46066b; role: concept -->

The rows come from 76 speakers with repeated productions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The criterion uses $n=1520$ token contributions because that is the likelihood fitted by the software. It does not imply that the study sampled that many independent speakers. The rows come from 76 speakers with repeated productions.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Interpreting the sample size

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture/13-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 643dad72ef0160bdfe257ca9c4073edd5f2d4d170c7512abaaf020126e46066b; role: concept -->

Thus, the values can rank these declared software fits, while their asymptotic evidence interpretation remains limited.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The usual BIC approximation presumes an appropriate independence structure. A token-level mixture that omits repeated-speaker dependence does not gain that structure from the penalty. Thus, the values can rank these declared software fits, while their asymptotic evidence interpretation remains limited.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Candidate-set and fit limits

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture/14-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/choosing-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 643dad72ef0160bdfe257ca9c4073edd5f2d4d170c7512abaaf020126e46066b; role: concept -->

Mixture label permutations and weakly represented components also complicate the regularity assumptions behind simple information-criterion arguments.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

BIC compares only the supplied component counts, covariance families, representation, and fitting controls. It cannot repair omitted F3 information, within-speaker dependence, or an unsuitable Gaussian family. Mixture label permutations and weakly represented components also complicate the regularity assumptions behind simple information-criterion arguments.

[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Reconstructing the data and speaker folds

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/validating-a-mixture/03-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/validating-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 130b31c4c2ddb9202bbe7601d91d5164ae57db8a96a2818e7e078999239ed3c5; role: concept -->

The target is thus an adapted complete panel, not a first isolated token.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The folds exclude every one of a held-out speaker’s 20 rows from mixture estimation. Each held-out speaker supplies an unlabeled panel for within-speaker standardization. The target is thus an adapted complete panel, not a first isolated token.

## Held-out log loss {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/validating-a-mixture/04-math; notes-page: latent-structure/validating-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 130b31c4c2ddb9202bbe7601d91d5164ae57db8a96a2818e7e078999239ed3c5; role: math -->

For a mixture fit to training speakers, the log loss of token $i$ is

$$
L_i(M)
=
-\log p_M
(\mathbf{x}_i\mid D_{\mathrm{train}}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a mixture fit to training speakers, the log loss of token $i$ is

$$
L_i(M)
=
-\log p_M
(\mathbf{x}_i\mid D_{\mathrm{train}}).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: latent-structure/validating-a-mixture.qmd
:::

## Held-out log loss {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/validating-a-mixture/05-math; notes-page: latent-structure/validating-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 130b31c4c2ddb9202bbe7601d91d5164ae57db8a96a2818e7e078999239ed3c5; role: math -->

Smaller loss means that the fitted model assigns greater density to the held-out acoustic vector. For two candidates $A$ and $B$, the paired token difference is

$$
d_i=L_i(B)-L_i(A).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Smaller loss means that the fitted model assigns greater density to the held-out acoustic vector. For two candidates $A$ and $B$, the paired token difference is

$$

$$

Because speakers are the held-out groups, we first average token losses within speaker and compare the resulting paired speaker means.

## Information-set and dependence limits

<!-- generated-slide-id: latent-structure/validating-a-mixture/12-concept; notes-page: latent-structure/validating-a-mixture.qmd; note-sha256: 130b31c4c2ddb9202bbe7601d91d5164ae57db8a96a2818e7e078999239ed3c5; role: concept -->

Speaker-level paired values describe the variation relevant to the claim without pretending that repeated folds create new speakers.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The mixture likelihood still treats transformed token rows as conditionally independent and does not model their shared speaker normalization. Fold averages are computational summaries, not independent samples. Speaker-blocked log loss slightly favors G14 on average, while external alignment favors K10 in every fold. This disagreement is informative because the criteria evaluate different consequences of the same label-blind acoustic fits.
